beats.script_body: We begin at the gilded statue of General William Tecumseh Sherman, best known for his bloody march through the South in the fall of 1864, when, as the Union's commander in the West, he burned large portions of Georgia and South Carolina. Sherman showed little remorse at Georgia's fate; as he famously put it, "War is cruelty and you cannot refine it." Walking before him, waving an olive branch, is the figure of Victory. The pine branch on the granite pedestal signifies Georgia, and the horses stomping on the pines are a painful reminder of the destruction of Sherman's March.

beats.script_body: The award-winning statue was cast by the well-known New York sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens and presented in 1900 at the Paris Exposition. It was erected in its present location in 1903, on a base by Charles McKim of McKim, Mead and White. The statue was regilded in the late 1980s to considerable complaint, as Sherman's bloody history was by then seen as unseemly — a gleaming gold tribute to a man remembered for burning the South.

beats.script_body: The Pulitzer Fountain, in the plaza in front of the Plaza Hotel, was erected in 1916 with a fifty-thousand-dollar gift from Joseph Pulitzer, who hoped to outdo his newspaper-magnate rival William Randolph Hearst. The statue on top is Pomona, the Greek goddess of abundance, finished by Karl Bitter, protégé of architect Richard Morris Hunt. The day he finished the clay model in 1915, Bitter was tragically killed crossing the street as he left the Metropolitan Opera, then on Forty-seventh Street, and his apprentices were left to complete the statue.

beats.script_body: The Plaza, dating from 1907, is one of New York's great luxury hotels. Frank Lloyd Wright, who hated New York, would stay only here when he passed through; other luminaries who made it their temporary residence included the Beatles, Mark Twain, Groucho Marx, and Eleanor Roosevelt. The very first guest to sign the Plaza's register was Alfred Gwynne Vanderbilt — who would later lose his life in the sinking of the Lusitania. The French Renaissance building was designed by Henry Hardenbergh, the same architect responsible for the Dakota.

beats.script_body: J. Pierpont Morgan formed the Metropolitan Club here, on the northeast corner of Fifth Avenue and Sixtieth Street, in anger. Some of his close comrades and fellow captains of industry had been unable to win entrance into the other elite clubs of the time, principally the Union Club. Morgan had proposed John King, president of the Erie Railroad, whose "career and character have won him the universal respect of all who know him" — but it was said King's table manners were not up to snuff, and he was promptly denied membership. Morgan's retribution was to get New York's most famous architect, Stanford White, to build "the largest, most imposing, and most luxurious of the clubhouses of New York." Morgan, it is said, summoned White with the words "Damn the expense." In its temerity to challenge the Union Club, the Metropolitan was dressed in an all-marble facade. One lure to new members was a dining room set aside for female guests — the Ladies Restaurant, overlooking the courtyard. Joining Morgan were Cornelius Vanderbilt and Robert Goelet.

beats.script_body: Across from the Metropolitan Club stands the Harmonie Club at 4 East Sixtieth Street. It was formed in 1852 by the German Jewish community as the Harmonie Gesellschaft — the Harmony Society — and was distinguished by having German as its official language and by hanging the kaiser's portrait in its hall. It was the first men's club in the city to admit women at dinner, and the first eventually to have women as members. The club dates from a period when the chasm between first-wave German Jews and the second-wave Eastern Europeans was massive, and many Harmonie denizens, eager to assimilate, had little desire to associate with their poorer brethren from the East.

beats.script_body: In October 1961, New York City detectives Eddie Egan and Sonny Grosso were having drinks after work at the Copacabana when they noticed a "little man in a silk suit, with a diamond stickpin in his tie, flashing a huge bankroll." They decided to follow him. The chase would last eighteen months and turn into The French Connection: in the end there were nine arrests, and a hundred and twelve pounds of heroin were secured — thirty-two million dollars' worth in 1960s dollars. The film's famous car-chase scene was shot over five weeks under Brooklyn's Bensonhurst Elevated, at full speed, with real pedestrians and traffic.

beats.script_body: The Copacabana was a venue for New York's stage and sports celebrities and for the average New Yorker alike — the stuff of high-school proms, college balls, and first dates. May 1957 saw one of its more notorious nights. With Sammy Davis Jr. on the stage and Yankee Billy Martin celebrating his twenty-ninth birthday alongside Mickey Mantle, Yogi Berra, and Hank Bauer, a brawl broke out between the Yankee players and a New Jersey bowling team. Police charges were ultimately dropped, but the Yankees' owner blamed Martin and traded him that July to Kansas City; he would not return until the 1970s, as the team's manager.

beats.script_body: The Grolier Club, at 47 East Sixtieth Street, is — in contrast with the business-titan appeal of the Metropolitan down the road — a club for book lovers. It was named for the sixteenth-century bibliophile Jean Grolier de Servières and founded for "the literary study and promotion of the arts pertaining to the production of books." Bertram Goodhue, best known for St. Bartholomew's Church next to the Waldorf Astoria, designed the clubhouse in 1916. The original Grolier Club stands at 29 East Thirty-second Street.

beats.script_body: Madison Avenue, one of New York City's narrowest avenues, is named for America's fourth president, who sadly died in 1836 — the year of the avenue's opening. It has a curious history, going from a predominantly residential thoroughfare to an outstanding commercial zone; because of zoning, many of its fashionable stores are now housed in the very townhouses and brownstones that survive from its residential days. Of the tour's three avenues, Madison emerged first, and it turned headfirst toward the commercial, becoming in the early postwar period the advertising capital of the world. No longer the center of advertising, it has reinvented itself, at least here, as "Boutique Row."

beats.script_body: The low building on the northeast corner of Sixty-second and Madison was originally Louis Sherry's restaurant, where to take tea was to "see a certain number of Our Best People." Sherry made his money as a first-class confectioner to the rich. His restaurant was better known for its antics — including the 1903 dinner for the New York Horseback Riding Club, sponsored by Chicago millionaire Cornelius Billings, at which diners ate on horseback. The tab? A mere fifty thousand dollars.

beats.trigger_address: west side of Madison Avenue near Sixty-second Street
beats.script_body: Although there is no plaque, across Madison Avenue on the west side stood the home where Theodore Roosevelt lived from 1895 to 1897, during his tenure as police commissioner of New York. As commissioner, he forced the resignation of the chief of the uniformed police, who had justified amassing $300,000 from "successful stock picks." Roosevelt took to prowling the streets at night in a black cape, hunting for policemen shirking their duty. The strolls made for good public relations, but his popularity suffered when he enforced the Sunday blue laws and closed the saloons; New Yorkers were happy to see him move on in 1897 to become assistant secretary of the navy.

beats.source_passage: Although there is no plaque, across Madison Avenue on the west side stood the home that Theodore Roosevelt lived in from 1895to 1897, during his tenure as police commissioner of New York... As commissioner, he forced the resignation of the chief of the uniformed police, who had justified recently amassing $300,000as the result of successful stock picks. Roosevelt adopted the practice of prowling the streets at night, dressed in a black cape, looking for policemen shirking their duty. While these strolls made for good public relations, his popularity suffered when he insisted on enforcing the Sunday blue laws, closing saloons. New Yorkers were happy to see him move on when, in 1897, he accepted President William McKinley's appointment as assistant secretary of the navy.

beats.script_body: The fabulous beaux-arts townhouse at 11 East Sixty-second Street is the Fabbri Mansion, commissioned and built in 1900 for William Vanderbilt's eldest daughter, Margaret Louisa Vanderbilt Shepard, who presented it to her daughter Edith and her son-in-law. The name Fabbri is for Edith's husband — note the F's designed into the wrought-iron balconies. Inside survive a wholly original nineteenth-century interior, with 1890s mahogany paneling in a twenty-five-by-forty-one-foot dining room, and walk-in safes and coal bins untouched for generations. The Fabbris left after only a year, preferring the more bucolic Carnegie Hill.

beats.script_body: A few doors from the Fabbri Mansion, at 5 East Sixty-second Street, is the Fifth Avenue Synagogue, with mid-1950s cat's-eye windows of elliptical stained glass. The architect, Percival Goodman, met the challenge of the narrow lot through the traditional Sephardic layout, which calls for a bimah and ark in a clear central area with facing sections of worshipers — a centralized plan that, unlike the more common arrangement where rabbi and cantor face the audience from the front, lets congregants better hear the service. Goodman, brother of the social critic Paul Goodman with whom he wrote Communitas, designed more than fifty synagogues in all.

beats.script_body: The Knickerbocker Club, on the southeast corner of Fifth Avenue and Sixty-second Street, was founded in 1871 as a reaction to the eased entry requirements at other clubs. It was Washington Irving who coined the word knickerbocker for New York's most socially prominent families — those who could trace their line to the original Dutch settlers — in his 1809 comic history, A History of New York, attributed to the imaginary Dutch-American scholar "Dietrich Knickerbocker." The book became part of New York folklore. Among the club's founders were Alexander Hamilton's grandson, John Jacob Astor, and Moses Lazarus, father of Emma Lazarus.

beats.script_body: The apartment house at 810 Fifth, greeting you with a grand iron marquee, was laid out with just one apartment per floor at an average of five thousand square feet. Its best-known resident to New Yorkers was former governor Nelson Rockefeller, who was so charmed by the building that he lived here with both his first and second wives. In 1963, Richard Nixon bought the fifth-floor apartment, shortly after Nelson and his second wife, Happy, moved in. Five years later the two men were dueling Republican candidates for the nomination — and during the battle they used different elevators to reach their respective apartments.

beats.script_body: Just inside Central Park at Sixty-fourth Street stands the Arsenal, built 1848 to 1851 — one of only two structures in the park that predate the park itself. When built it housed the majority of New York State's ammunition during the war with Mexico, set deliberately four miles from City Hall as a safety measure. During the Civil War it served as a bunkhouse for Union troops, and later became, in turn, the city's Museum of Natural History, park headquarters, a police station, and a weather observatory; since 1934 it has housed the city's Parks headquarters. Look for the eagle over the door and the pyramids of cannonballs on the facade.

beats.script_body: The famous Wildenstein Gallery, at 19 East Sixty-fourth Street, was founded in Paris in 1875 by Nathan Wildenstein, who left his native Alsace after the Franco-Prussian War to remain a French citizen. Raphael's Madonna and Child and Van Gogh's Entrance to the Public Garden at Arles are but two of the thousands of works sold over the years to major museums and collectors. The building itself was built in 1932 by Horace Trumbauer with Julian Abele — one of the few Black architects working in a major firm at that time, and the lead architect of the Duke University campus in North Carolina.

beats.script_body: The Seventh Regiment Armory, built by Charles Clinton in 1877 to 1880, is the only serious holdover from when the New York Central Railroad came barreling down Fourth Avenue. The socially prominent Seventh Regiment had formed in 1806 and, in 1824, became the first regiment to adopt the term National Guard; in 1874 the city leased this site to it, and the regiment raised the money for a monumental new armory. This extravagantly turreted red brick and brownstone structure became the prototype for the medieval-inspired armories built across New York for the next fifty years. The wealth of the regiment shows in its interiors: Louis Tiffany, Stanford White, and the Herter Brothers all worked on rooms here, and all ten companies hired the foremost New York design firms for their second-floor company rooms, fitted out with Renaissance woodwork, ornamented piano alcoves, stained glass, and parquet floors. The drill room — two hundred by three hundred feet and one hundred feet high — is one of the largest unobstructed spaces in New York. And the building is still a living, breathing armory, where you'll often see National Guardsmen amid Sunday-afternoon antique enthusiasts.

beats.script_body: Sara Roosevelt, mother of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, commissioned Charles Adams Platt to design the twin buildings at 47–49 East Sixty-fifth Street in 1907, shortly after FDR married Eleanor — a wedding present. The two homes share a single entranceway and have interconnecting doors, though Eleanor was not fond of Sara's penchant for bursting in, as she often did. Franklin and Eleanor lived here on and off for some twenty years, and it was in the fourth-floor bedroom that FDR convalesced from polio in 1921 and 1922. After Sara's death in 1941, the building was purchased for use by Hunter College.

beats.script_body: Temple Emanu-El, at 840 Fifth Avenue on the corner of Sixty-fifth Street, is the largest Reform synagogue in the world, edging out the Dohány synagogue in Budapest. The congregation, formed in 1845, joined with Temple Beth-El in 1927. On this very site once stood Richard Morris Hunt's double-size mansion for the Mrs. Astor — Caroline Schermerhorn Astor — and, alongside it, the home of her son John Jacob Astor; both masterpieces came down to make way for the synagogue. Built in a Byzantine and Romanesque style that mixes western European and Near Eastern forms, the building is particularly expressive of the Jewish diaspora. Its main sanctuary rises to a hundred and three feet — St. Patrick's Cathedral, by contrast, is a hundred and eight — and the auditorium runs a hundred and fifty feet long. The side walls are among the largest load-bearing masonry walls anywhere, carrying huge transverse steel beams. Step inside at 1 East Sixty-fifth Street: the rose window, stained glass, mosaics, and marble podium are otherworldly.

beats.script_body: The Frick Collection, at 1 East Seventieth Street, is the Indiana-limestone former home of art collector, coal magnate, and union buster Henry Clay Frick, designed by Carrère & Hastings, architects of the New York Public Library. Frick is infamous for helping instigate the 1892 crackdown on the Homestead strikers at the Carnegie Steel plant; he was also fearful that the Pittsburgh fumes would tarnish his prized works. John Russell Pope turned the building into a museum in the 1930s, and the central court with its fountain is one of the city's finest public spaces. The galleries hold Vermeers, Rembrandts, Titians, and Bellinis — and by the gallery's charter, nothing travels.

beats.script_body: Directly opposite the Frick, between Seventieth and Seventy-first Streets, stands the Richard Morris Hunt Memorial, commemorating one of America's most influential architects. Hunt is known for the base of the Statue of Liberty, the Fifth Avenue facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and numerous mansions; he was also the first American trained at the École des Beaux Arts in Paris. Colleagues erected this monument in 1898, and Daniel Chester French, of Lincoln Memorial fame, sculpted the bronze bust and the two female figures — the left representing Art, the right Architecture. The figure on the right holds a replica of one of Hunt's buildings from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the "White City."

beats.script_body: On the northeast corner of Sixty-ninth Street and Park Avenue, at 701 Park, is the prestigious Union Club. Founded in 1836 by men from the top echelons of New York's upper crust, it is the city's oldest social club — and the very one that kept out J. P. Morgan's comrades. Many of the younger clubs in the city descend from it. One in particular, the Union League Club, was founded by Republicans who left the Union Club in 1863, incensed by its failure to expel Confederate sympathizers. Morgan, we now see, was not alone in his grievance.

beats.script_body: The Asia Society, on the northeast corner of Park and Seventieth Street, was founded in 1956 by John D. Rockefeller III to foster understanding between Asians and Americans — and to house his massive Asian art collection. Asia House on East Sixty-fourth Street was its first home; in 1981 the Society moved here, into a building of red sandstone from Rajasthan, India and polished granite from Oklahoma, the combination of stones itself meant to illustrate the cooperation between Asia and America.

beats.script_body: The radio- and television-broadcasting pioneer David Sarnoff lived in the six-story, thirty-room townhouse at 44 East Seventy-first Street until his death in 1971, having risen from a five-dollar-and-fifty-cent-a-week office boy to chairman of RCA and later NBC. On April 14, 1912, Sarnoff was working the Marconi station atop Wanamaker's department store on Eighth Street when he picked up a relayed message: "S.S. Titanic ran into iceberg, sinking fast." For the next seventy-two hours, the story goes, he stayed at his post, giving the world its first authentic news of the disaster.

beats.script_body: The Gertrude Rhinelander House, now Polo Ralph Lauren, stands at 867 Madison on the corner of Seventy-second Street. The Rhinelanders made their fortune in colonial-era sugar; their Rhinelander Sugar House, behind the present Municipal Building downtown, became a brutal prison for American soldiers during the British occupation of 1776 to 1783. Gertrude herself never got to live here — her husband died while it was being built, and she couldn't afford to keep it.

beats.script_body: Across Madison Avenue stands the imposing, perhaps out-of-place Whitney Museum of American Art, designed by Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer and built between 1963 and 1966. It houses the twentieth-century collection of Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, great-granddaughter of Cornelius "Commodore" Vanderbilt. A sculptor and patron, Whitney bought and exhibited John Sloan, Edward Hopper, and Stuart Davis early in their careers. By 1929 her collection ran to hundreds of master works, and she offered it to the Metropolitan Museum of Art — which declined. So she set up her own museum, placing primacy on latter-day artists.

beats.source_passage: Across Madison Avenue is the imposing, and perhaps out-of-place, Whitney Museum of American Art. Designed by Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer and built between 1963to 1966, the Whitney houses the twentieth-century art collection of Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney (1875–1942). ...Whitney was a sculptor and patron of American art and bought and exhibited painters such as John Sloan, Edward Hopper, and Stuart Davis early in their careers. By 1929her collection contained hundreds of twentieth-century master works. At that time she approached the Metropolitan Museum of Art to see if they had interest in permanently exhibiting her collection; the Met declined her offer. Whitney instead decided to exhibit her collection on its own merits and set up a museum that placed primacy on latter-day artists.

beats.script_body: Begin at the gilded statue of General William Tecumseh Sherman, at Fifty-ninth Street and Fifth Avenue, the southeast corner of Central Park. From here you'll walk a lower slice of the Upper East Side — up to Seventy-fifth Street, weaving through Fifth, Madison, and Park Avenues. Much of what you'll see falls within the Upper East Side Historic District, designated in 1981.

Much of the area you will see is now part of the Upper East Side Historic District, which runs from Fifty-ninth Street to Seventy-eighth...and was designated in 1981.

beats.script_body: Cross to the east side of Park and walk north to the Armory. As you go, picture this avenue's past: from dirt road to railroad to road of riches. In the 1830s it was filled with track for the New York and Harlem Railroad and known as Fourth Avenue; only after the New York Central electrified its line in 1907, sinking the tracks underground, did Park become the landscaped boulevard its name implies.
key_claims: Park Avenue went from dirt road to railroad to boulevard
In the 1830s it carried the NY and Harlem Railroad and was called Fourth Avenue
NY Central electrified in 1907, sinking tracks underground
beats.source_passage: On reaching Park Avenue, cross and walk north along the east side of Park to the Armory. ...From dirt road to railroad to road of riches, Park Avenue has gone through several prominent permutations... In the 1830s, the road was filled with railroad track and became known as Fourth Avenue. ...With the New York Central Railroad's transition from steam to electric in 1907, the railroad lines were put underground and Park Avenue became, as its name implies, a beautifully landscaped boulevard with dignified apartment houses.

review_queue.description: New POI 'Fabbri Mansion' (11 E 62nd St) is almost certainly the SAME building as existing POI 'Edith and Ernesto Fabbri House' in the context list. The book names 'Edith's husband' Fabbri; the existing POI is named for Edith and Ernesto Fabbri. They are within ~0m.
review_queue.recommendation: Do NOT create a duplicate POI. At poi-generate/dedup time, alias 'Fabbri Mansion' to existing 'Edith and Ernesto Fabbri House' and attach the Fabbri beat to that POI. NOTE: that existing Fabbri House POI may be a different Fabbri residence (the Fabbris owned 7 E 95th in Carnegie Hill too) — verify the address before merging.

review_queue.description: New POI 'Union Club' (701 Park / 101 E 69th) was tentatively listed with matched_existing='Knickerbocker Club' to surface it, but it is a DISTINCT, genuinely new POI (it is explicitly the rival that rejected Morgan's circle). No Union Club currently exists in the POI list.
review_queue.recommendation: Treat Union Club as a genuinely new POI; matched_existing should be null. Create at poi-generate time.

review_queue.description: New POI 'Copacabana (10 East 60th Street site)' sits on the same East 60th Street block (between Fifth and Madison) as new POIs 'Harmonie Club' (4 E 60th) and 'Grolier Club' (47 E 60th), and existing 'Metropolitan Club' (1 E 60th) — several within ~100m.
review_queue.recommendation: Keep distinct (different addresses on a long block) but flag for user review per the 100m guardrail. The original Copacabana building is demolished; consider whether to retain it as a pop-culture/crime POI or fold its beats into a block-level container.

review_queue.description: Book internal inconsistency: it places BOTH the Copacabana AND 'Hotel 14' at '14 East Sixtieth Street' in adjacent sentences ('The Copacabana was at 14 East Sixtieth Street' then 'Next door to the Copacabana, at 14 East Sixtieth, was Hotel 14'). The Copa's historic address is 10 East 60th. Geocoded the Copa POI block-level on East 60th between Fifth and Madison (MEDIUM confidence).
review_queue.recommendation: Use block-level geofence for the Copacabana POI; do not trust the verbatim '14 East Sixtieth' number. Hotel 14 was extracted-skipped as a minor walk-by with no standalone narrative.

review_queue.description: Minor date discrepancy (not auto-corrected, not a dispute): the book dates the Whitney's Breuer building 'built between 1963 to 1966'; secondary sources give construction 1964–66 (opened 1966). The 1966 completion is correct. Difference is the construction-start year only.
review_queue.recommendation: Keep source-faithful text. No correction; flagged informationally.

review_queue.description: Grolier Club building completion: book says Goodhue 'designed the club in 1916'; sources confirm 1916 commission/lot acquisition with construction completed December 1917. Both are consistent (design 1916, built 1916–17). Kept as written.

Dense walk chunk: ~30 distinct stops in the source; many minor walk-by mentions (Sherry Netherland, Bergdorf Goodman, Christ Church, Central Presbyterian, Lotos Club, New India House, 515/610/630/820/912 Fifth/Park residences, Colony Club detail, Jimmy Walker, Lillian Hellman, Arnold Rothstein, Berwind house, Verona, Harkness House, Pulitzer's 73rd-St mansion, Council on Foreign Relations, Hunter College) were extracted-skipped or compressed to keep the beat count <=25 and focus on the strongest, fully-grounded stories. POIs for Christ Church, Colony Club, Lotos Club, Central Presbyterian, Wildenstein were geocoded for future passes even where no beat was emitted this run.
review_queue.recommendation: A future pass (or larger beat budget) could harvest the skipped residences (Jimmy Walker '610 Park', Lillian Hellman '630 Park', Arnold Rothstein '912 Fifth', Berwind '2 E 64th', Verona '32 E 64th', Edward Harkness House '1 E 75th', Joseph Pulitzer Mansion '11 E 73rd') as additional seasoning/famous_residents beats.
